description: Fundamentalism, the Scopes Trial, Jim Crow, the reborn KKK and the Great Migration north.
content_html:
Religious Fundamentalism and the Bible Belt

In many parts of rural America, particularly across the southern and mid-western states, Protestant Christianity was more than a private belief — it shaped schooling, politics and daily life. This region, stretching from Texas to Virginia, became known as the Bible Belt. For religious fundamentalists, the Bible was the literal word of God, to be accepted without question. Darwin’s theory of evolution was seen as a direct challenge to the Biblical account of creation in Genesis.

The conflict between religion and modern science exploded into public view in 1925. Tennessee had passed the Butler Act that year, making it illegal to teach evolution in state-funded schools. A young biology teacher named John Scopes deliberately challenged the law by teaching evolution to his class in Dayton, Tennessee. His arrest and trial became a national sensation.

Key Fact

The 1925 Scopes Trial in Dayton, Tennessee, pitted William Jennings Bryan (fundamentalist) against Clarence Darrow (defence) over the teaching of evolution. Scopes was convicted and fined $100, but the trial exposed fundamentalism to national ridicule and was broadcast live on radio to millions of Americans.

The prosecution was led by William Jennings Bryan, a three-time presidential candidate and devout fundamentalist. The defence was led by Clarence Darrow, one of the most famous lawyers in America. The trial became a clash of worldviews: Bryan argued that the Bible must govern what was taught in schools; Darrow argued that freedom of thought and scientific inquiry must not be sacrificed to religious doctrine.

Scopes was convicted and fined $100 (the verdict was later overturned on a technicality). However, the real verdict went to the modernists. Broadcast live on radio, the trial allowed millions to hear Darrow cross-examine Bryan directly on the Bible — an embarrassing experience for Bryan, who struggled to answer questions about the age of the Earth. Bryan died five days after the trial ended. Although fundamentalism did not disappear, its influence on national politics weakened after 1925.

Segregation and Jim Crow

For African Americans, the 1920s were years of profound inequality. Across the South, Jim Crow laws enforced the separation of Black and white Americans in schools, transport, restaurants, hospitals and courtrooms. The 1896 Supreme Court decision in Plessy v. Ferguson had declared “separate but equal” facilities constitutional, providing legal cover for systematic discrimination.

In practice, Black facilities were rarely equal. Schools for Black children received a fraction of the funding allocated to white schools. Voting rights were suppressed through poll taxes, literacy tests and the constant threat of violence. Lynching — the murder of Black people, usually by hanging, by white mobs — was used as a weapon of terror. Between 1882 and 1968, approximately 3,446 Black Americans were lynched, according to records compiled by the NAACP. The 1920s saw a peak of racial violence, including the Tulsa Race Massacre of 1921, in which a prosperous Black neighbourhood was destroyed by a white mob.

Key Fact

The revived Ku Klux Klan, re-founded in 1915, reached a peak membership of approximately 4–5 million by the mid-1920s. Unlike the original post-Civil War Klan, the 1920s Klan targeted not only Black Americans but also Catholics, Jews, immigrants and trade unionists, and had significant political influence in several states.

The Rebirth of the Ku Klux Klan

The original Ku Klux Klan was founded in the South after the Civil War to terrorise newly freed Black Americans. It was largely suppressed by the 1870s. In 1915, it was revived by William Joseph Simmons at Stone Mountain, Georgia, partly inspired by the racist film The Birth of a Nation. The 1920s Klan was a mass movement, not just a fringe organisation. It attracted millions of members across the North and Midwest as well as the South, appealing to working-class white Protestants who felt threatened by immigration, urbanisation and social change.

The Klan used terror — beatings, arson and murder — but also operated openly through marches, political endorsements and church events. By 1924 it had significant influence in the Democratic Party’s national convention. Its power declined sharply after 1925, when a prominent Klan leader, David Stephenson, was convicted of the murder of a young woman in Indiana. The scandal drove many members away. However, the Klan’s violence had already caused immense harm.

African Americans organised to resist racism in different ways. The NAACP (National Association for the Advancement of Colored People), founded in 1909, campaigned through legal challenges and lobbying for anti-lynching legislation. Although Congress blocked an anti-lynching bill in the 1920s, the NAACP kept pressure on lawmakers and publicised racial violence to northern audiences.

Marcus Garvey offered a different vision. His UNIA (Universal Negro Improvement Association) promoted Black pride, economic self-help and, ultimately, the idea that African Americans should return to Africa to build an independent nation. Garvey attracted hundreds of thousands of followers, particularly in urban Black communities. He was imprisoned in 1925 on fraud charges and deported in 1927, but his ideas influenced later Black nationalist movements.

The most significant response to southern racism was migration. In the Great Migration, approximately 1.6 million Black Americans moved north and west between 1910 and 1930, seeking factory work in cities like Chicago, Detroit and New York, and escaping the worst of Jim Crow segregation. This migration created vibrant Black urban communities and was the foundation of the Harlem Renaissance.
exam_tip_html: When answering questions about religion and race, be precise about which group you are discussing and what their actual actions or beliefs were — examiners deduct marks for vague generalisations like “Black people were treated badly.” For 8-mark significance questions, address significance at the time (the KKK’s terror campaign, the Scopes Trial broadcast nationally) and over time (long-term impact on civil rights movement, fundamentalism in politics). For extended essays on whether the United States was truly a ‘nation of contrasts’, the experience of Black Americans in the 1920s is your strongest evidence of the gap between the “roaring twenties” image and the reality for millions of citizens.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Religious fundamentalism, centred in the Bible Belt, clashed with scientific modernism in the 1925 Scopes Trial. Scopes was convicted, but the trial broadcast nationally on radio exposed fundamentalism to ridicule and weakened its national influence.
  • Jim Crow laws enforced racial segregation across the South, backed by the threat of lynching. The revived KKK reached 4–5 million members by the mid-1920s, targeting Black Americans, Catholics, Jews and immigrants before its decline after the Stephenson scandal in 1925.
  • African Americans responded through the NAACP (legal challenges), Marcus Garvey’s UNIA (Black pride and self-help), and the Great Migration of approximately 1.6 million people from the South to northern cities between 1910 and 1930.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Ku Klux Klan in the 1920s.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for identifying a feature; one mark for supporting detail.
Example: The Klan reached a peak membership of approximately 4-5 million in the mid-1920s [1], attracting members not only in the South but also across northern and mid-western states, targeting Black Americans, Catholics, Jews and immigrants [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Jim Crow system in the southern United States.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per feature: one for the feature, one for supporting detail.
Feature 1: Jim Crow laws enforced racial segregation in public life — schools, transport, restaurants and hospitals were separated, legally justified by the Supreme Court's 1896 'separate but equal' ruling in Plessy v. Ferguson. [2]
Feature 2: Voting rights for Black Americans were suppressed through poll taxes, literacy tests and the threat of violence — lynching was used as a weapon of terror, with approximately 3,446 Black Americans lynched between 1882 and 1968 according to NAACP records. [2]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the Ku Klux Klan grew so rapidly in the early 1920s.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains a precise cause with specific factual support and a clear causal chain.
Secure: Valid cause with supporting evidence and a developed explanatory link.
Developing: Names a cause but explanation is brief or generic.
Emerging: Simple statement.
Valid causes: fear of immigration and urban change among white Protestants; economic competition from Black workers migrating north; the 1915 film 'The Birth of a Nation' romanticising the original Klan; nativist and anti-Catholic sentiment; weak law enforcement response to Klan violence.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Great Migration for African Americans in the United States.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Traces a consequence with precise evidence and clear analysis of how migration produced that outcome.
Secure: Valid consequence with supporting detail.
Developing: Names a consequence without full explanation.
Emerging: Simple point.
Valid consequences: creation of vibrant Black urban communities in Chicago, Detroit and New York; escape from Jim Crow segregation and lynching; basis for the Harlem Renaissance; increased political visibility of Black communities; continued discrimination in northern cities (housing, work).

practice_questions.text:
How significant was the 1925 Scopes Trial in revealing tensions within American society in the 1920s?
Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Addresses significance at the time and over time with precise evidence and sustained analysis.
Secure: Explains significance with relevant supporting detail.
Developing: Some explanation; may address only one dimension.
Emerging: Simple points without developed analysis.
At the time: broadcast on radio to millions, exposing fundamentalism to national ridicule; revealed a deep rural-urban, religious-secular divide; Bryan's embarrassment under cross-examination; Scopes convicted but fine later overturned.
Over time: fundamentalist political influence weakened nationally; demonstrated the tension between religious tradition and scientific modernity that persisted in American culture.

practice_questions.text:
'Marcus Garvey's UNIA was a more effective response to racism in the 1920s than the NAACP.'
How far do you agree with this interpretation? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Agrees and disagrees with specific evidence for both positions, reaching a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Makes points for and against with relevant evidence; judgement present.
Developing: Unbalanced or lacks a clear judgement.
Emerging: Simple agreement or disagreement.
Agreement (Garvey more effective): attracted hundreds of thousands of followers quickly; promoted positive Black identity and economic self-sufficiency; gave African Americans pride and a vision for the future.
Disagreement (NAACP more effective): used legal channels to challenge discrimination; sustained campaign over decades; kept anti-lynching legislation in public debate; Garvey imprisoned 1925 and deported 1927, leaving UNIA weakened.
Judgement: NAACP had longer-lasting institutional impact; Garvey's movement collapsed with his imprisonment.

glossary_terms.definition: The area of the southern and mid-western United States where Protestant fundamentalist Christianity was dominant in public and cultural life.
A movement among conservative Protestants who insisted on the literal truth of the Bible and rejected scientific theories they believed contradicted it.
A system of racial segregation laws in the southern United States that enforced the separation of Black and white Americans in public life from the 1870s to the 1960s.

A white supremacist organisation founded in the South after the Civil War, revived in 1915 and reaching peak membership of 4-5 million in the mid-1920s, targeting Black Americans, Catholics, Jews and immigrants.
National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, founded in 1909, which campaigned through legal challenges and political pressure for civil rights.
Universal Negro Improvement Association, founded by Marcus Garvey in 1914, which promoted Black pride, Black economic self-sufficiency and a return to Africa.
The movement of approximately 1.6 million Black Americans from the rural South to northern and mid-western cities between 1910 and 1930.
